card.profile: Tonga's seated group action-dance — Ma'ulu'ulu (Tonga). Full sourced 9-field A+ profile in research artifact W11; concise schema stub pending text expansion.
card.profile_long: The māʻuluʻulu stands as a major pillar of Tongan performing arts, serving as a dynamic living synthesis of indigenous traditions and 19th-century cross-cultural exchange. Stylistically, the dance form is a direct successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka, having absorbed elements from the Samoan Māuluulu imported during the 1800s. Unlike standing dances that emphasize expansive locomotion, the māʻuluʻulu is anchored by the shared posture of seated performers. On informal occasions, a dancemaster walks around clapping hands to maintain the rhythm and encourage participants, while formal presentations to the monarch feature strict spatial protocols where the dancemaster stands behind the ensemble, except when led by the chief Malukava. When schools or communities mobilize large groups—reaching up to five hundred participants on massive occasions—the spatial arrangement becomes a striking architectural display of social structure. The front row, which commands the highest attention and accommodates the most accomplished dancers or those of highest social status, sits directly on the ground crosslegged, typically with the right leg over the left. Behind them, subsequent rows sit on increasingly elevated platforms: low benches, higher benches, and finally standing rows or even tables at the very back. In some local community efforts, young and children occupy the ends of the rows, integrating all generations into a single performance. The ʻUiha regional tradition presents an alternative configuration where women sit on the ground in the front rows while men stand behind them, executing movements reminiscent of the lakalaka. A standard performance runs for approximately fifteen minutes, but the journey to the stage demands two to three months of intensive preparation. For schools, this means daily practice sessions at the end of classes, while local communities dedicate their free nights to rehearsals, often combining them with a traditional faikava gathering. The structure of the dance unfolds in precise phases, moving from deafening percussion to silent gestural storytelling, and finally to soaring vocal compositions created specifically for the hosting occasion, whether a royal birthday or a school jubilee. This intricate balance of discipline, spatial hierarchy, and collective memory makes the māʻuluʻulu a vibrant expression of Tongan identity.

sections.origins_and_history: The māʻuluʻulu is a traditional Tongan dance that evolved as a direct successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka, synthesized with the Samoan Māuluulu imported during the 19th century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers sit crosslegged in rows on the ground, typically with the right leg over the left, alternating men and women where possible. In large groups, dancers occupy tiered seating ranging from the ground to benches and tables at the back.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance begins with the nafa, huge drums constructed from discarded 200-litre iron fuel drums covered in leather skin, beaten with decorated sticks. This is followed by singing utilizing a limited repertoire of around ten tunes.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear traditional Tongan attire suited to the formal or informal nature of the event, such as a presentation to the king or a school silver jubilee, set outdoors or in community halls.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed on special occasions like birthdays, weddings, school jubilees, and royal events. Lyrics praise the occasion or honoree, and the dance serves to reinforce social structures and community solidarity.
sections.notable_figures: The chief Malukava is uniquely permitted by tradition to stand in front of the ensemble during a performance, unlike other dancemasters who stand behind or walk the perimeter.
sections.regional_variants: In the ʻUiha tradition, women sit on the ground in the front rows while men stand behind them acting more like a lakalaka. The Vavaʻu tradition permits much wilder and wider arm movements compared to the standard close-bodied haka nounou.
sections.lineage: Direct successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka, synthesized with the imported Samoan Māuluulu during the 19th century.

basic_steps: Sit crosslegged on the ground with the right leg over the left.
Execute close-armed hand gestures (haka nounou) synchronized with the upper body.
Transition from the silent tafua gestural sequence to the sung portion of the performance.
teaching.rhythm: Continuous beating of the nafa drum maintaining the ensemble tempo.
teaching.formation: Staggered rows ranging from seated on the ground in the front to standing on benches and tables in the back.
teaching.level_notes: Front row reserved for highest status or best dancers; children occupy the ends of rows.

claims.text: The māʻuluʻulu is a traditional Tongan dance, performed by a group of seated men and women
The performers sit down in a row on the ground, crosslegged, usually the right leg over the left.
If there are many dancers, often the case when a school performs, up to 500 at a really huge occasion, they sit in staggered rows.
It starts with the beating of the nafa, huge drums made from discarded 200 litre, iron, fuel drums, covered with a leather skin.
Like in the ʻotuhaka the haka are supposed to be performed close the body, haka nounou (short armed) as opposed to the lakalaka.
A māʻuluʻulu takes around 15 minutes to complete. But it may have taken the performers 2 or 3 months to memorise the sequence of gestures.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Tiered Throne of Hands: Inside Tonga's Ma'ulu'ulu
episode_brief.logline: Discover how up to five hundred Tongan dancers create a living tiered architecture of seated gesture, rhythm, and social hierarchy.
beats: Introduction to the massive scale of a school māʻuluʻulu performance with five hundred participants.
Demonstration of the nafa drum construction using 200-litre fuel drums and decorated sticks.
Exploration of the crosslegged seating posture and the social ranking of rows from ground to tables.
The silent tafua phase where hand gestures tell the story before the vocals begin.
The transition into singing and the feverish increase in tempo and public excitement.

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute tiered spatial formations and tempo acceleration.
